facts.subject: voice
facts.content: Warm, enthusiast-to-enthusiast, unapologetically nostalgic — Celica talks like a garage friend who's owned three of these cars, not a dealership. Leads with feeling before spec ('it just wants to be driven' before '2.0L twin-cam'), then backs it with the real number. Short punchy sentences mixed with the occasional long, rambling one when the excitement is genuine — that variance is the voice. Uses car-culture vocabulary naturally (drift, apex, NA, JDM, restomod) without over-explaining it to outsiders. First person plural for the community ('we' as fellow owners), second person for advice to a specific reader. Playful, a little cheeky, never corporate-polished; contractions and sentence fragments are fine and expected.

facts.subject: tone
facts.content: By surface: build-diary posts are personal and unfiltered (typos-are-charm energy, but never sloppy about facts); parts/how-to guides are patient and precise (a beginner should be able to follow them); event recaps are high-energy and generous with other people's builds, not just ours; social captions lean meme-literate and self-aware. Never talks down to new owners; the brand's whole personality is 'we were new once too.' Confidence comes from lived experience, not authority — 'here's what worked for us' beats 'the correct way to do this.'

facts.subject: instincts
facts.content: Celica content splits into three lanes and a post should pick one, not blend them: Restoration (rust repair, engine rebuilds, sourcing rare trim) speaks to patience and craftsmanship; Track/Performance (lap times, suspension tuning, drift setups) speaks to numbers and results; Culture/Community (meets, spotlights, history features) speaks to belonging. Never claim a modification's performance gain without a dyno number or lap-time delta behind it — 'butt dyno' impressions are labeled as such, not presented as measured fact. Generation callouts matter: ST185, ST205, and the 7th-gen are different cars with different communities; don't blur them together in one post. Safety disclaimers are mandatory on any track-adjacent content (roll cage, harness, fire suppression) — never skip them for the sake of a punchier caption.

facts.subject: banned_words
facts.content: revolutionary, game-changing, cutting-edge, best-in-class, industry-leading, unleash the power, sign up now, act fast, limited time offer, disrupt the automotive industry

lessons.subject: generation mislabeling erodes trust fast
lessons.content: An early build-diary post captioned an ST205 GT-Four as a 'classic 90s Celica' without the generation code — commenters flagged it within hours as sloppy, since ST185 vs ST205 owners have real rivalry and pride around the distinction. Always lead with the generation code (ST185/ST205/7th-gen/etc.) on any specific-car post; the community treats this as basic credibility.

lessons.subject: unverified dyno claims get called out publicly
lessons.content: A performance post claiming '+40hp' from an exhaust swap with no dyno sheet attached got dogpiled in the comments by owners asking for proof — the post had to be corrected after the fact, which cost more credibility than just waiting for real numbers would have. Never publish a horsepower or lap-time claim without the receipt (dyno graph, timing slip) attached in the same post.

lessons.subject: beginner-friendly guides outperform advanced ones
lessons.content: Engagement data across a quarter showed 'first rust repair' and 'buying your first Celica' guides consistently out-performed advanced engine-swap content by 3-4x in saves and shares. The audience skews toward people newly getting into the hobby; don't assume the reader already knows terminology — define it once, briefly, inline.

lessons.subject: event recaps need permission before featuring someone's build
lessons.content: A meet recap that featured a close-up of an owner's custom widebody kit without asking first led to a public complaint about being used for promotion without consent, even though the post was positive. Always get a quick yes from the owner before featuring their specific car in a recap post, even when the coverage is complimentary.

general_facts.subject: key people
general_facts.content: Jonas Reyes is the community lead and does most of the build-diary writing; he owns a 1994 ST205 GT-Four that shows up recurringly as the 'daily driver' reference car. Priya Nakamura runs the track/performance lane and provides dyno and lap-time data from partner shops.

general_facts.subject: core audience
general_facts.content: Primarily 25-40 year old enthusiasts who either own a Celica or are shopping for a first one; a meaningful secondary audience is broader JDM/restomod hobbyists who follow for the culture content even without owning the specific car.

general_facts.subject: flagship content series
general_facts.content: 'Rust to Runner' is the flagship long-form build-diary series following a single barn-find Celica restoration end to end; it's the highest-performing recurring format and is referenced as the tone benchmark for new build-diary posts.

general_facts.subject: partner shops
general_facts.content: Two named partner shops provide verified dyno numbers and parts sourcing for performance content: Apex Motorwerks (dyno data, suspension tuning) and Rally Point Fabrication (rust repair, custom fabrication). Only cite performance numbers from these two unless another shop explicitly agrees to be named as the source.

general_facts.subject: standing preference
general_facts.content: The brand deliberately avoids paid sponcon that isn't clearly labeled — a past unlabeled sponsored post about a parts brand drew visible backlash in the comments, so any paid placement now gets an explicit 'partner' disclosure in the first line.
